extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors and course designers who give and assess student mathematical writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for giving feedback and designing assessment/rubrics for student writing in mathematics courses (small assignments, drafts, and major projects), including strategies for commenting, grading, and encouraging substantive revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose-driven commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider your purpose for commenting and craft your comments to achieve that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether comments are aimed at improving mathematical accuracy, exposition, motivation, revision skills, or other goals, and tailor the content and level of detail of comments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer in-person feedback when feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet with each student to provide feedback when possible, since feedback given in person is often more efficient and richer than written comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although scheduling can be difficult, face-to-face meetings allow instructors to understand students better as writers and to hear student responses to comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out strengths (positive feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out what the student does well; positive feedback is remarkably effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance criticism with recognition of strengths to motivate revision and help students understand successful strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the text at multiple scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the text at all scales: it’s easy to overlook large issues when you’re focused on details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give feedback not only on sentence-level correctness but also on organization, argument structure, and high-level coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize feedback to match student learning capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how much the student can learn in the available time and decide what the student most needs to learn at this point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid listing every problem; schedule multiple revisions so large-scale issues may be addressed first and smaller-scale issues later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight the most important comments in a summary
rubrics_metrics.description: If you provide many comments, help students recognize relative importance by drawing attention to key issues in a summary note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a brief front-page summary or prioritized list so students know where to focus their revision energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coded comments to de-emphasize minor issues
rubrics_metrics.description: De-emphasize less important issues through the use of coded comments (examples from MIT are provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes let students rapidly identify priority vs. minor problems without reading numerous marginal notes in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mark every instance of a recurring problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of marking each occurrence of a repeated error, tell the student how to identify and fix the problem themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encourages self-editing and prevents overburdening the student with repetitive corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triage distracting local errors during reading
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are distracted by an error while reading, briefly note it on scratch paper or a temporary document, then continue reading and decide afterward which issues to comment on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents small errors from monopolizing the reviewer’s attention and ensures a focus on higher-priority feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: When no revision will occur, give generalizable comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the writing will not be revised, limit comments to general guidance that will apply to future writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid detailed line edits when students won't have an opportunity to rework the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage use of a personal editing checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest that students keep an editing checklist of mistakes they often make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A checklist helps students self-correct recurring problems and track progress across assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dictating solutions; refer to the text, not the student
rubrics_metrics.description: When pointing out problems, refer to the text rather than making it personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase comments as suggestions about the writing (e.g., “This paragraph could be more concise.”) rather than criticisms of the student’s abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions to comment on: correctness, clarity, flow, organization
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenting, consider mathematical correctness, clarity, flow and organization, and other general principles of communicating mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance verbosity, instructor time investment, and usefulness; these dimensions can structure both marginal comments and summary feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide class-wide feedback as an alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to individualized feedback, give feedback to the whole class when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post common issues and guidance to the class (e.g., guidance for revising an algorithm assignment) to address widespread problems efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and prioritize grading criteria before grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide and prioritize grading criteria prior to grading to prevent unintentional subconscious bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a rubric or grading sheet; see guidance pages and a grading handbook with sample lists and rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rubrics to make expectations explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students with a rubric or sample of what you are looking for so they know effective communication will be evaluated and contribute to their grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving a rubric before the assignment encourages students to 'write to the rubric'; instructors new to assessing writing may omit a rubric for the first assignment to learn baseline student performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-grade approach for small writing assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign two grades for small writing assignments: one for mathematical content and one for quality of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To save time, an overall exposition grade may be used instead of grading exposition on each problem; make students aware that communication counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grade the full project lifecycle for large projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Grade proposal, intermediate drafts, peer-review, and the final product when evaluating large writing projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making the grading process transparent helps students understand expectations and encourages continuous improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft grading strategy: effort + advisory rubric grade
rubrics_metrics.description: For drafts, assign two grades: one based on effort/completeness (the grade that counts) and an advisory grade based on the rubric for the final paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rewards effort while giving students actionable feedback about how much improvement is needed for the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final paper grading components — correctness of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctness of mathematics should be explicitly graded for final papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the validity of proofs, calculations, and logical reasoning as a distinct criterion from writing quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final paper grading components — clarity of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of exposition should be graded as a distinct dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how clearly ideas, explanations, and arguments are communicated to the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final paper grading components — flow and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Flow and organization of the paper should be a separate grading criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the logical ordering of ideas, transitions between sections, and the reader’s ability to follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final paper grading components — extent feedback was incorporated
rubrics_metrics.description: Grade the extent to which instructor and peer feedback was addressed in revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including this in the grade encourages students to take feedback seriously and demonstrates improvement across drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow rubrics to be teaching tools; be cautious with rigid grids
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rubrics not only as assessment tools but also as teaching tools; a detailed grading grid is an option but may not capture diverse strengths/weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing mathematics is complex; a precise grid may fail to represent important qualitative differences among students' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging major revisions: give high-level comments for major issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If major revision is needed, give only high-level comments so students focus on big-picture changes rather than details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed comments may cause students to focus on surface fixes and miss necessary structural or conceptual rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly tell students what to 'rewrite' versus 'revise'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly indicate which sections should be rewritten as opposed to merely revised, and define these terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear direction helps students understand the magnitude of the required changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scheduling revision at the end of term
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid placing revision deadlines at the end of term when students are pressed for time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide adequate time for meaningful revision and for students to consult with instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet individually to support revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet with students individually to allow questions about feedback and to signal the importance of writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-on-one attention increases student buy-in and clarifies expectations for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model major revision by sharing instructor drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: If you show students drafts of your own writing that exhibit major revision, students will better appreciate the need for substantive rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling instructor revision practices demystifies the process and normalizes substantial rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require student self-assessment and a revision plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students assess the quality of their writing and submit a revision plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-assessment increases metacognition; a plan forces students to prioritize changes and articulate their revision strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require documentation of changes and explanations for non-changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Require students to indicate which changes they made in revision and explain why certain changes were not made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accountability helps instructors see student decision-making and motivates thorough revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include incorporation of peer/instructor comments in the grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Include in the grade the extent to which instructor and peer comments were addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy incentivizes students to engage with feedback and complete substantial revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing 'writing-to-learn' — prioritize process feedback over summative grading
rubrics_metrics.description: If an assignment’s purpose is to help students learn mathematics (writing-to-learn), provide feedback on the process rather than primarily grading writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback and revision cycles to stimulate rethinking and intellectual growth; consider low-stakes or formative assessment models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using writing to assess understanding — validity and teacher linguistic awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: When using writing as evidence of students' mathematical activity, consider whether the writing accurately presents their understanding and whether instructors have sufficient linguistic awareness to support students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious interpreting written work; support students' language development and be mindful that writing skill and mathematical understanding are distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-informed caution: feedback focus shapes student revision priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Research indicates students revise most on aspects emphasized by instructor comments (e.g., if professor only comments on grammar, revisions focus on grammar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the kinds of improvements you value to guide student revision toward deeper mathematical and expository goals.
